How to use this

The full ISC 2027 Paper I syllabus (Mathematics 860), unit by unit. Each chapter gives the concepts, the standard results with their proofs, the diagrams, a formula sheet, a worked example for every question type the forecast ranks as probable (working and answer behind Show working), the common errors, and a most probable in 2027 note drawn from the 2017–2026 board papers, the 2018–2027 specimens and the CISCE competency booklet. The tag beside each example id is the slot it fits (A1 = Section A, 1 mark; B2, C3, D5 likewise). Every answer was recomputed in sympy.

Not in the 2027 syllabus, so not here: linear regression and correlation, calculus in commerce and economics, the binomial distribution and variance of a random variable, Rolle’s and Lagrange’s theorems, L’Hospital’s rule, approximation by differentials, inverse by elementary row operations, the scalar triple product, the family of planes through a line of intersection, and solving second-order differential equations.

1 · Relations and Functions

Unit 1 · 10 marks with inverse trig (about 7 for relations and functions) · Section A 1-markers on relations; a 5-mark functions case study in Section D

ConceptRelations

  • A relation on a set A is any subset of A × A. The empty relation is φ, the universal relation is A × A, the identity relation is {(a, a) : a ∈ A}.
  • Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A. Symmetric: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R. Transitive: (a, b), (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R.
  • An equivalence relation is all three. It splits A into disjoint equivalence classes [a] = {x : (x, a) ∈ R}.
  • To disprove a property one counter-example is enough; to prove it you must argue for arbitrary elements.

Reflexive is about every element of A; symmetric and transitive are conditional — a relation with no pairs to test is vacuously symmetric and transitive.

ConceptFunctions

  • f : A → B is a relation in which every a ∈ A has exactly one image. A is the domain, B the codomain, f(A) the range.
  • One-one (injective): f(x1) = f(x2) ⇒ x1 = x2. Graphically: every horizontal line meets the graph at most once.
  • Onto (surjective): range = codomain. Graphically: every horizontal line through the codomain meets the graph.
  • Invertible ⇔ one-one and onto (bijective). Then f−1 : B → A, and the graph of f−1 is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.
  • Composite (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)) needs range f ⊆ domain g; in general g∘f ≠ f∘g.
  • Counting for |A| = m, |B| = n: functions nm; one-one maps n(n−1)…(n−m+1) if m ≤ n, otherwise 0; bijections m! if m = n, otherwise 0.
  • A many-one function can be made invertible by restricting the domain to a piece on which it is monotonic — the idea behind the 2027 case study.

DiagramOne-one and onto in arrow diagrams

One-one: no element of B receives two arrows. Onto: every element of B receives an arrow (the grey d receives none). Not a function: 1 has two images and 3 has none.

DiagramA function and its inverse

DerivationThe inverse of a bijection is unique

To prove. if g and h are both inverses of f : A → B, then g = h.

  1. g∘f = IA and f∘h = IB, by definition of inverse.
  2. For every y ∈ B: g(y) = g(IB(y)) = g(f(h(y))) = (g∘f)(h(y)) = IA(h(y)) = h(y).
g = h, so the inverse, when it exists, is unique.

DerivationComposite of one-one functions is one-one

To prove. f : A → B and g : B → C one-one ⇒ g∘f one-one.

  1. Let g(f(x1)) = g(f(x2)).
  2. g one-one ⇒ f(x1) = f(x2); f one-one ⇒ x1 = x2.
g∘f is one-one. (The same argument with “onto” shows g∘f is onto when both are.)

Worked examples

Worked exampleClassify a relation given by a rule (specimen 2027 Q1(i))

R1 A1

R on ℤ is given by a R b ⇔ a2 − 7ab + 6b2 = 0. Is R reflexive, symmetric, transitive?

Show working
  1. Factorise: a2 − 7ab + 6b2 = (a − b)(a − 6b), so a R b ⇔ a = b or a = 6b.
  2. Reflexive: a = a always, so (a, a) ∈ R. ✓
  3. Symmetric: (6, 1) ∈ R since 6 = 6·1, but (1, 6): 1 ≠ 6 and 1 ≠ 36. ✗
  4. Transitive: (36, 6) and (6, 1) are in R, but (36, 1): 36 ≠ 1 and 36 ≠ 6. ✗

Answer reflexive only — neither symmetric nor transitive.

Worked exampleA relation with a single pair (specimens 2025, 2026)

R2 A1

A = {a, b, c}, R = {(b, b)}. Classify R.

Show working
  1. Reflexive needs (a, a), (b, b), (c, c); (a, a) is missing. ✗
  2. Symmetric: the only pair (b, b) reverses to itself. ✓
  3. Transitive: (b, b), (b, b) ⇒ (b, b) ∈ R. ✓

Answer symmetric and transitive, not reflexive

Worked exampleProve an equivalence relation and find a class (NCERT Ex 1.1)

R3 B2

A = {0, 1, 2, …, 12}, R = {(a, b) : |a − b| is a multiple of 4}. Show R is an equivalence relation and write the class of 1.

Show working
  1. Reflexive: |a − a| = 0 = 4 · 0.
  2. Symmetric: |b − a| = |a − b|.
  3. Transitive: a − b = 4k, b − c = 4l ⇒ a − c = 4(k + l).
  4. Class of 1: all x ∈ A with x − 1 a multiple of 4.

Answer equivalence relation; [1] = {1, 5, 9}

Worked exampleProve bijective and find the inverse (B2023 Q2)

R4 B2

f : ℝ − {2} → ℝ − {1}, f(x) = x − 1x − 2. Show f is one-one and onto and find f−1.

Show working
  1. One-one: x1 − 1x1 − 2 = x2 − 1x2 − 2 ⇒ x1x2 − 2x1 − x2 + 2 = x1x2 − x1 − 2x2 + 2 ⇒ x1 = x2.
  2. Onto: y = x − 1x − 2 ⇒ x = 2y − 1y − 1, defined for every y ≠ 1, and this x ≠ 2 (x = 2 would give −1 = 0).
  3. So every y in the codomain has a pre-image.

Answer f is a bijection and f−1(x) = 2x − 1x − 1

Worked exampleInverse of a cubic expression (B2026 Q3)

R5 B2

f(x) = 4 − (x − 7)3, f : ℝ → ℝ. Find f−1.

Show working
  1. f is strictly decreasing (a negative cube), so one-one; a cubic takes every real value, so onto.
  2. y = 4 − (x − 7)3 ⇒ (x − 7)3 = 4 − y ⇒ x = 7 + (4 − y)1/3.

Answer f−1(x) = 7 + (4 − x)1/3

Worked exampleFunctions case study — the 2027 D-slot (specimen 2027 Q16, new data)

R6 D5

f(x) = x2 − 4x + 5, x ∈ ℝ. (i) Find the range. (ii) Why has f no inverse on ℝ? (iii) g is f restricted to (−∞, 2]; find g−1 and g−1(5). (iv) h is f restricted to [2, ∞); find h−1(5). (v) Solve g−1(x) = h−1(x).

Show working
  1. (i) f(x) = (x − 2)2 + 1 ≥ 1, minimum 1 at x = 2: range [1, ∞).
  2. (ii) f(1) = f(3) = 2: not one-one (a horizontal line cuts twice).
  3. (iii) On x ≤ 2, x − 2 = −√(y − 1), so g−1(x) = 2 − √(x − 1), x ≥ 1; g−1(5) = 2 − 2 = 0. Check g(0) = 5. ✓
  4. (iv) h−1(x) = 2 + √(x − 1); h−1(5) = 4 (check h(4) = 5).
  5. (v) 2 − √(x − 1) = 2 + √(x − 1) ⇒ √(x − 1) = 0.

Answer range [1, ∞); g−1(5) = 0; h−1(5) = 4; x = 1

Worked exampleThe specimen case study itself (specimen 2027 Q16)

R7 D5

f(x) = x − 6√x + 1, x ≥ 0. g = f on [0, 9], h = f on [9, ∞). Find g−1, h−1, and solve g−1(x) = h−1(x).

Show working
  1. Complete the square in √x: f = (√x − 3)2 − 8, minimum −8 at x = 9.
  2. On [0, 9], √x ≤ 3: √x = 3 − √(y + 8), so g−1(x) = (3 − √(x + 8))2.
  3. On [9, ∞): h−1(x) = (3 + √(x + 8))2.
  4. Equal ⇔ 3 − √(x + 8) = ±(3 + √(x + 8)); the + sign forces √(x + 8) = 0, the − sign 6 = 0.

Answer g−1(x) = (3 − √(x + 8))2, h−1(x) = (3 + √(x + 8))2; x = −8

Worked exampleCounting functions (B2026 Q1(ix), S2021)

R8 A1

|A| = 3, |B| = 4. How many functions, one-one functions and onto functions A → B?

Show working
  1. Functions: each of 3 elements has 4 choices: 43.
  2. One-one: 4 · 3 · 2.
  3. Onto: 3 elements cannot cover 4 images.

Answer 64 functions, 24 one-one, 0 onto

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Calling R reflexive because (a, a) holds for the elements that happen to appear in R: it must hold for every element of A.
  • Proving onto by solving for x but not checking that x lies in the domain (the x ≠ 2 step in R4).
  • Writing the inverse on the wrong branch: on x ≤ 2 the square root comes with a minus sign.
  • Treating f−1(x) as 1/f(x).
  • Forgetting that the domain of f−1 is the range of f.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • Section A (2 marks): classify a relation by a rule or by listed pairs (R1, R2) — in the 2027 specimen and three of the last four boards; one-one/onto read from a graph; f and f−1 as reflections in y = x (specimen Q1(xvi)).
  • Section D (5 marks): the functions case study — natural domain, why no inverse, inverse on each monotonic piece, verify f∘f−1, solve the two inverses equal (R6, R7). Variants to expect: x + 4/x, (x − 1)2 + 3, 2x3 − 3x2 − 12x + 8.
  • Find f−1 of a rational or cubic map (R4, R5): set in B2023, B2024 and B2026 in turn.

2 · Inverse Trigonometric Functions

Unit 1 · about 3 marks · A 1-mark MCQ on range or principal value and a 2-mark evaluate/solve

ConceptPrincipal branches

FunctionDomainPrincipal range
sin−1 x[−1, 1][−π/2, π/2]
cos−1 x[−1, 1][0, π]
tan−1 xℝ(−π/2, π/2)
cot−1 xℝ(0, π)
sec−1 xℝ − (−1, 1)[0, π] − {π/2}
cosec−1 xℝ − (−1, 1)[−π/2, π/2] − {0}

sin−1(sin x) = x only for x in [−π/2, π/2]; outside it, bring the angle back into the principal range first.

DiagramThe principal branches

Each is the reflection in y = x of the restricted trigonometric graph. Note the closed ends of sin−1 and cos−1 and the asymptotes of tan−1.

Derivationsin−1x + cos−1x = π/2

To prove. for x ∈ [−1, 1].

  1. Let sin−1x = θ, so x = sin θ = cos(π/2 − θ), θ ∈ [−π/2, π/2].
  2. Then π/2 − θ ∈ [0, π], the principal range of cos−1, so cos−1x = π/2 − θ.
sin−1x + cos−1x = π/2; likewise tan−1x + cot−1x = π/2 and sec−1x + cosec−1x = π/2.

Caution the step “π/2 − θ lies in [0, π]” is the whole proof — always check the range.

DerivationAddition formula for tan−1

To prove. tan−1x + tan−1y = tan−1x + y1 − xy when xy < 1.

  1. Let tan−1x = α, tan−1y = β, both in (−π/2, π/2).
  2. tan(α + β) = tan α + tan β1 − tan α tan β = x + y1 − xy.
  3. When xy < 1, α + β lies in (−π/2, π/2), so we may take tan−1 of both sides.
tan−1x + tan−1y = tan−1x + y1 − xy (xy < 1); tan−1x − tan−1y = tan−1x − y1 + xy (xy > −1).

Caution for x, y > 0 with xy > 1 the sum is π + tan−1x + y1 − xy.

DerivationThe 2 tan−1x formulae

To prove. 2 tan−1x = sin−12x1 + x2 (|x| ≤ 1) = cos−11 − x21 + x2 (x ≥ 0) = tan−12x1 − x2 (|x| < 1).

  1. Put x = tan θ, θ ∈ (−π/2, π/2).
  2. sin 2θ = 2 tan θ1 + tan2θ, cos 2θ = 1 − tan2θ1 + tan2θ, tan 2θ = 2 tan θ1 − tan2θ.
  3. Each inversion is legitimate only when 2θ is in the principal range of that function: 2θ ∈ [−π/2, π/2] ⇔ |x| ≤ 1; 2θ ∈ [0, π] ⇔ x ≥ 0; 2θ ∈ (−π/2, π/2) ⇔ |x| < 1.
All three equal 2 tan−1x on their stated intervals. Similarly 2 sin−1x = sin−1(2x√(1 − x2)) for |x| ≤ 1/√2, 3 tan−1x = tan−13x − x31 − 3x2 for |x| < 1/√3.

Worked examples

Worked examplePrincipal values (B2026 Q1(xiv), S2023 Q1(iii))

T1 A1

Find sec−1(−√2) and tan−1√3 − sec−1(−2).

Show working
  1. sec−1(−√2) = cos−1(−1/√2) = π − π/4.
  2. tan−1√3 = π/3; sec−1(−2) = cos−1(−½) = 2π/3.

Answer sec−1(−√2) = 3π/4; tan−1√3 − sec−1(−2) = −π/3

Worked exampleRange of an ITF expression (specimen 2027 Q1(ii))

T2 A1

θ = sin−1x + cos−1x − tan−1x, x ≥ 0. Find the least and greatest values of θ.

Show working
  1. θ = π/2 − tan−1x.
  2. The domain is fixed by sin−1: 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, so 0 ≤ tan−1x ≤ π/4.

Answer π/4 ≤ θ ≤ π/2

Worked exampleSolve an ITF equation (B2023 Q5)

T3 B2

Solve 5 tan−1x + 3 cot−1x = 2π.

Show working
  1. cot−1x = π/2 − tan−1x.
  2. 5 tan−1x + 3π/2 − 3 tan−1x = 2π ⇒ tan−1x = π/4.

Answer x = 1

Worked exampleTwo-root ITF equation (specimens 2025, 2026 Q7)

T4 B2

Solve sin−1x + sin−1(1 − x) = cos−1x.

Show working
  1. sin−1(1 − x) = cos−1x − sin−1x = π/2 − 2 sin−1x.
  2. Take sine: 1 − x = cos(2 sin−1x) = 1 − 2x2.
  3. 2x2 − x = 0 ⇒ x = 0 or ½. Both check in the original equation.

Answer x = 0 or x = ½

Worked exampleDomain forces the value (specimen 2027 Q6(ii))

T5 B2

ax2 + sin−1(x2 − 2x + 2) + cos−1(x2 − 2x + 2) = 0 has a real root. Find x and a.

Show working
  1. x2 − 2x + 2 = (x − 1)2 + 1 ≥ 1, and sin−1 needs it ≤ 1: so it equals 1 and x = 1.
  2. Then sin−11 + cos−11 = π/2, and a(1) + π/2 = 0.

Answer x = 1, a = −π/2

Worked exampleITF sum in a right triangle (specimen 2027 Q6(i))

T6 B2

In △PQR, ∠R = 90° and p, q, r are the sides opposite P, Q, R. Show tan−1pq + r + tan−1qr + p = π/4.

Show working
  1. Both arguments are positive and their product pq/((q + r)(r + p)) < 1, so the addition formula applies.
  2. Numerator of the combined fraction: p(r + p) + q(q + r) = p2 + q2 + r(p + q) = r2 + r(p + q), using r2 = p2 + q2.
  3. Denominator: (q + r)(r + p) − pq = r2 + r(p + q).
  4. The fraction is 1 and tan−11 = π/4.

Answer the sum is π/4

Worked exampleMixed ITF evaluation (B2026 Q8(ii))

T7 B2

Find x if 2 tan−1(1/3) + sec−1(5√2/7) = tan−1x.

Show working
  1. 2 tan−1(1/3) = tan−12/31 − 1/9 = tan−1(3/4).
  2. sec θ = 5√2/7 ⇒ tan θ = √(50/49 − 1) = 1/7, so sec−1(5√2/7) = tan−1(1/7).
  3. tan−1(3/4) + tan−1(1/7) = tan−125/2825/28.

Answer x = 1

Worked exampleTrigonometric value of an ITF expression (B2020 Q3(b))

T8 B2

Evaluate cos(2 cos−1x + sin−1x) at x = 1/5.

Show working
  1. 2 cos−1x + sin−1x = cos−1x + π/2.
  2. cos(π/2 + φ) = −sin φ with cos φ = 1/5, so sin φ = √24/5.

Answer value = −2√6/5

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Taking sin−1(sin 2π/3) = 2π/3: the principal value is π/3.
  • Ignoring the domain of the ITF (T2, T5): the domain is often the whole question.
  • Using the tan−1 sum formula when xy > 1 without adding π.
  • cos−1(−x) = −cos−1x is false; it is π − cos−1x.
  • Not checking roots: squaring or taking sine can introduce roots that fail the original equation.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • A1: range or bounds of a combined expression (T2) and a principal value (T1); statement or A–R items on tan−1(tan x) = x (true only on (−π/2, π/2)).
  • B2: the specimen slot is an ITF sum in a context (T6) or a domain-forced equation (T5); boards have set “solve an ITF equation” (T3, T4, T7) in six consecutive years.
  • ITF drops from 6–8 marks to about 3 in 2027: no 4-mark identity proofs are expected.

3 · Matrices and Determinants

Unit 2 · 10 marks · two A1s, a 3-mark determinant proof or matrix application, a 5-mark system by A−1

ConceptMatrices

  • Types: row, column, square, diagonal, scalar (kI), identity, zero, upper/lower triangular.
  • A is symmetric if AT = A, skew-symmetric if AT = −A (so its diagonal is zero). Every square matrix is uniquely ½(A + AT) + ½(A − AT).
  • AB exists when columns of A = rows of B. In general AB ≠ BA, and AB = O is possible with A, B ≠ O — so (A + B)2 ≠ A2 + 2AB + B2 and AB = AC does not give B = C unless A is invertible.
  • (AB)T = BTAT; (AB)−1 = B−1A−1.

ConceptDeterminants, adjoint, inverse

  • Minor Mij: delete row i and column j. Cofactor Cij = (−1)i+jMij. |A| = a11C11 + a12C12 + a13C13 (any row or column).
  • adj A = (Cij)T; A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A| I; A−1 = adj A / |A| when |A| ≠ 0.
  • For an n × n matrix: |kA| = kn|A|, |adj A| = |A|n−1, |A−1| = 1/|A|, |AT| = |A|.
  • System AX = B: |A| ≠ 0 ⇒ unique solution X = A−1B (consistent). |A| = 0: if (adj A)B ≠ O inconsistent (no solution); if (adj A)B = O, infinitely many or none — check the equations.
  • Area of a triangle with vertices (xi, yi) is ½|Δ| with Δ = x1y11x2y21x3y31; collinear ⇔ Δ = 0.

DerivationProperties of determinants

To prove. the six properties used to “evaluate without expanding”, for a 3 × 3 determinant.

  1. P1 (transpose): expanding |A| by row 1 and |AT| by column 1 gives the same six terms, so |AT| = |A|; every row property is therefore a column property too.
  2. P2 (swap): swapping two rows reverses the sign. Each of the six terms a1pa2qa3r carries the sign of the permutation (p q r); a swap changes the parity of every permutation.
  3. P3 (equal rows): if two rows are equal, swapping them leaves Δ unchanged but P2 says it becomes −Δ, so Δ = −Δ = 0.
  4. P4 (factor): multiplying one row by k multiplies every term of the expansion along that row by k, so Δ becomes kΔ.
  5. P5 (split): if each entry of a row is a sum, expand along that row: each cofactor multiplies (b + c), so Δ splits into two determinants.
  6. P6 (row operation): Ri → Ri + kRj. By P5 the result is Δ plus a determinant whose row i is k × row j; by P4 and P3 that one is k · 0.
Δ is unchanged by Ri → Ri + kRj; changes sign on a swap; is 0 with two equal (or proportional) rows; scales by k with one row scaled by k.

DerivationUniqueness of the inverse (a syllabus line never yet set)

To prove. a square matrix has at most one inverse.

  1. Let B and C both be inverses of A: AB = BA = I and AC = CA = I.
  2. B = BI = B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C (associativity of multiplication).
B = C.

DerivationA(adj A) = |A| I and hence A−1

To prove. for a 3 × 3 matrix A, A(adj A) = |A| I3.

  1. The (i, j) entry of A(adj A) is ai1Cj1 + ai2Cj2 + ai3Cj3 (row i of A times column j of adj A = row j of the cofactors).
  2. i = j: this is the expansion of |A| along row i, so it equals |A|.
  3. i ≠ j: it is the expansion of a determinant whose row j has been replaced by row i — two equal rows — so it is 0 (“expansion by alien cofactors”).
  4. Hence A(adj A) = |A|I; similarly (adj A)A = |A|I. If |A| ≠ 0, divide by |A|.
A−1 = 1|A| adj A, which exists ⇔ |A| ≠ 0.

Derivation(AB)−1 = B−1A−1

To prove. for invertible A, B of the same order.

  1. (AB)(B−1A−1) = A(BB−1)A−1 = AIA−1 = I.
  2. Likewise (B−1A−1)(AB) = I; by uniqueness this is the inverse.
(AB)−1 = B−1A−1 — note the reversal.

Worked examples

Worked exampleFit a quadratic model through three readings (specimen 2027 Q20 type)

M1 D5

A firm’s weekly profit (₹ thousand) in week t is P(t) = at2 + bt + c. P(1) = 6, P(2) = 11, P(3) = 18. Write the system as AX = B, find A−1, and hence a, b, c.

Show working
  1. a + b + c = 6, 4a + 2b + c = 11, 9a + 3b + c = 18, so A = 111421931, X = (a, b, c)T, B = (6, 11, 18)T.
  2. |A| = 1(2 − 3) − 1(4 − 9) + 1(12 − 18) = −1 + 5 − 6 = −2 ≠ 0, so a unique solution exists.
  3. Cofactors row by row: (−1, 5, −6), (2, −8, 6), (−1, 3, −2); adj A = −12−15−83−66−2.
  4. X = 1−2 adj A · B: first entry (−6 + 22 − 18)/(−2) = 1; second (30 − 88 + 54)/(−2) = 2; third (−36 + 66 − 36)/(−2) = 3.

Answer |A| = −2; a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, so P(t) = t2 + 2t + 3

Solve 2x + 3y + z = 37, x + 2y + 3z = 26, 3x + y + z = 37 by the matrix method.

Show working
  1. A = 231123311, |A| = 2(2 − 3) − 3(1 − 9) + 1(1 − 6) = −2 + 24 − 5 = 17.
  2. adj A = −1−278−1−5−571.
  3. X = 117 adj A · (37, 26, 37)T = 117(170, 85, 34)T.

Answer |A| = 17; x = 10, y = 5, z = 2

M3 D5

Solve 2x + 3y + 10z = 4, 4x − 6y + 5z = 1, 6x + 9y − 20z = 2.

Show working
  1. Put u = 1/x, v = 1/y, w = 1/z: A = 23104−6569−20.
  2. |A| = 2(120 − 45) − 3(−80 − 30) + 10(36 + 36) = 150 + 330 + 720 = 1200.
  3. adj A = 7515075110−10030720−24; (u, v, w) = 11200(600, 400, 240).

Answer u = ½, v = ⅓, w = ⅕, so x = 2, y = 3, z = 5

M4 C3

An order needs 150 ribbons and 20 covers. Company A charges ₹12 a ribbon and ₹180 a cover; B charges ₹10 and ₹200. Use matrices to decide which is cheaper.

Show working
  1. Quantity row [150 20]; price matrix with a column per company 1210180200.
  2. [150 20]1210180200 = [150·12 + 20·180  150·10 + 20·200].

Answer cost [5400  5500]: company A is cheaper by ₹100

Worked exampleA determinant identity by properties (B2025I Q7)

M5 C3

Prove 111abca3b3c3 = (a − b)(b − c)(c − a)(a + b + c).

Show working
  1. C1 → C1 − C2, C2 → C2 − C3: 001a − bb − cca3 − b3b3 − c3c3.
  2. Take (a − b) from C1 and (b − c) from C2: the columns become (0, 1, a2 + ab + b2) and (0, 1, b2 + bc + c2).
  3. Expand along R1: 1 · [(b2 + bc + c2) − (a2 + ab + b2)] = (c − a)(a + b + c).

Answer the determinant equals (a − b)(b − c)(c − a)(a + b + c)

Worked exampleFactorise a symmetric determinant (B2020 Q4)

M6 C3

Show xpqpxqqqx = (x − p)(x2 + px − 2q2).

Show working
  1. R1 → R1 − R2: row 1 becomes (x − p, p − x, 0) = (x − p)(1, −1, 0).
  2. Take out (x − p), then C2 → C2 + C1: row 1 = (1, 0, 0), rows (p, x + p, q), (q, 2q, x).
  3. Expand: (x + p)x − 2q2.

Answer Δ = (x − p)(x2 + px − 2q2)

  1. R2 → R2 + R3: every entry becomes a + b + c.

Answer the determinant is 0

M13 A1

Common errorsCommon errors

  • |2A| = 2|A| for a 3 × 3 matrix: it is 8|A|.
  • Forgetting to transpose the cofactor matrix when forming adj A.
  • Solving AX = B as X = BA−1: the inverse goes on the left.
  • Taking one sign only in ½|Δ| = area (M12).
  • Declaring “no solution” as soon as |A| = 0: you must also look at (adj A)B.
  • Taking a factor out of a row and a column at the same time and counting it once (specimen 2026 Q1(iv) A–R).

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • D5: a system from a real situation solved by A−1 = adj A / |A| (M1–M3) — the single most likely long question in the paper; the specimen fitted S(t) = at2 + bt + c through three readings.
  • C3: a determinant identity by properties (M5, M6) or a matrix-multiplication cost comparison (M4).
  • A1: |kA| / |adj A| (M8), complete a symmetric or skew matrix (M9), non-commutativity and AB = O (M13), consistency (M11), area/collinearity (M12).

4 · Continuity, Differentiability and Differentiation

Unit 3 (Calculus, 35 marks) · about 7 marks here · a 2-mark constants/graph question, a 3-mark second-derivative identity, 2 marks on an ITF-substitution derivative

ConceptContinuity

  • f is continuous at a if limx → a−f(x) = limx → a+f(x) = f(a) (all three exist and agree).
  • Removable discontinuity: the limit exists but f(a) is undefined or different — redefining f(a) removes it. Jump (non-removable): left and right limits exist but differ.
  • Sums, products, quotients (denominator ≠ 0) and composites of continuous functions are continuous. Polynomials, sin, cos, ex, log x (x > 0) and |x| are continuous on their domains; [x] jumps at every integer.

ConceptDifferentiability

  • f′(a) exists when LHD = limh → 0−f(a + h) − f(a)h equals RHD.
  • Differentiable ⇒ continuous; the converse fails: |x| at 0 (a corner), x1/3 at 0 (a vertical tangent).
  • For a piecewise function, the two conditions for differentiability at a joint are: the pieces meet (continuity) and their slopes agree.
  • x|x| is differentiable everywhere; |x − a| + |x − b| has corners at a and b and slope 0 between them.

DiagramReading a graph: hole, jump, corner

DerivationDifferentiability implies continuity

To prove. if f′(a) exists then f is continuous at a.

  1. f(a + h) − f(a) = f(a + h) − f(a)h · h for h ≠ 0.
  2. As h → 0 the right side tends to f′(a) · 0 = 0.
limh → 0f(a + h) = f(a): f is continuous at a.

DerivationDerivatives of ex and log x from first principles

To prove. d/dx ex = ex and d/dx log x = 1/x (x > 0), using limh → 0eh − 1h = 1 and limh → 0log(1 + h)h = 1.

  1. d/dx ex = limh → 0ex+h − exh = ex limh → 0eh − 1h = ex.
  2. d/dx log x = limh → 0log(x + h) − log xh = limh → 0log(1 + h/x)h/x · 1x = 1x.
d/dx ex = ex; d/dx log x = 1/x; hence d/dx ax = ax log a (write ax = ex log a).

DerivationDerivatives of sin−1x and tan−1x

To prove. d/dx sin−1x = 1√(1 − x2) (|x| < 1), d/dx tan−1x = 11 + x2.

  1. y = sin−1x ⇒ sin y = x, y ∈ (−π/2, π/2). Differentiate: cos y · y′ = 1.
  2. cos y > 0 on that interval, so cos y = +√(1 − sin2y) = √(1 − x2).
  3. y = tan−1x ⇒ tan y = x ⇒ sec2y · y′ = 1 ⇒ y′ = 1/(1 + tan2y) = 1/(1 + x2).
d/dx sin−1x = 1/√(1 − x2), d/dx cos−1x = −1/√(1 − x2), d/dx tan−1x = 1/(1 + x2).

Caution the sign of cos y is decided by the principal range — that is the step examiners look for.

DerivationThe second derivative of a parametric curve

To prove. if x = x(t), y = y(t) then d2ydx2 = ddt(dydx) ÷ dxdt, not (d2y/dt2)/(d2x/dt2).

  1. dydx = dy/dtdx/dt is a function of t; call it g(t).
  2. Chain rule: d2ydx2 = dgdx = dgdt · dtdx = g′(t) / x′(t).
d2ydx2 = g′(t)x′(t), where g(t) = y′(t)/x′(t).

Worked exampleConstants for differentiability (specimen 2027 Q5(i), new data)

D1 B2

f(x) = aex + b for x ≤ 0 and x2 + 3x + 2 for x > 0 is differentiable at 0. Find a and b.

Show working
  1. Continuity at 0: a + b = 0 + 0 + 2.
  2. LHD = ae0 = a; RHD = 2(0) + 3 = 3; equal ⇒ a = 3.

Answer a = 3, b = −1

Worked exampleContinuity: find k (B2024 Q4(i))

D2 A1

f(x) = (x + 3)2 − 36x − 3 (x ≠ 3), f(3) = k is continuous at 3. Find k.

Show working
  1. (x + 3)2 − 36 = (x + 3 − 6)(x + 3 + 6) = (x − 3)(x + 9).
  2. For x ≠ 3, f(x) = x + 9 → 12.

Answer k = 12

Worked exampleRead continuity from a graph (specimen 2027 Q5(ii))

D3 B2

For the graph in the diagram above (hole at −2, jump at 0, corner at 2), name the removable discontinuity and count the points where f is not differentiable.

Show working
  1. x = −2: the limit from both sides is 2 but f(−2) = 3·5 — removable.
  2. x = 0: left limit 3, right limit 1 — a jump, not removable.
  3. x = 2: both pieces meet at 2 with slopes ½ and −0·9 — continuous, not differentiable.

Answer removable at x = −2; not differentiable at 3 points (−2, 0, 2)

D4 C3

y = 3 cos(log x) + 4 sin(log x). Show x2y″ + xy′ + y = 0.

Show working
  1. xy′ = −3 sin(log x) + 4 cos(log x).
  2. Differentiate again: xy″ + y′ = [−3 cos(log x) − 4 sin(log x)]/x = −y/x.
  3. Multiply by x.

Answer x2y″ + xy′ + y = 0

Worked exampleSecond-derivative identity with a log (B2026 Q9)

D5 C3

y = x3 log(1/x). Show xy″ − 2y′ + 3x2 = 0.

Show working
  1. y = −x3 log x; y′ = −3x2 log x − x2.
  2. y″ = −6x log x − 3x − 2x = −6x log x − 5x.
  3. xy″ − 2y′ = −6x2 log x − 5x2 + 6x2 log x + 2x2 = −3x2.

Answer xy″ − 2y′ + 3x2 = 0

D9 C3

  2. Differentiate x2 + y2 = a2: y′ = −x/y.
  3. y″ = −(y − xy′)/y2 = −(y2 + x2)/y3.

Answer dy/dx = −x/y, d2y/dx2 = −(x2 + y2)/y3

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Checking only continuity (or only equal slopes) for differentiability at a joint: both are needed (D1).
  • d2y/dx2 = (d2y/dt2)/(d2x/dt2): wrong (D10).
  • Using tan−1(tan 2θ) = 2θ without checking that 2θ lies in (−π/2, π/2).
  • d/dx(xx) = x · xx−1: take logs first; the answer is xx(1 + log x).
  • Calling a hole a jump: removable means the limit exists.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • C3: a second-derivative identity — in every board from 2017 to 2026; the 2027 specimen used the substitution form (D6). Practise D4, D5, D9.
  • B2: constants for differentiability (D1), or reading removable/jump/corner points off a graph (D3) — four specimens in a row.
  • C3 part: an ITF-substitution derivative (D7), in the 2027 specimen paired with a local-maximum claim.
  • A1: continuity constant (D2), |x − a| + |x − b| (D13), parametric trap (D10), infinite radical (D11).

5 · Applications of Derivatives

Unit 3 · about 10 marks · four 1-mark items, a 5-mark case study (cubic model or related rates)

ConceptRates, monotonicity, tangents

  • Rate of change: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt). Differentiate the relation first, then substitute the instant’s values.
  • f′ > 0 on an interval ⇒ strictly increasing; f′ < 0 ⇒ strictly decreasing. Critical points: f′ = 0 or f′ undefined.
  • Tangent at (x1, y1): y − y1 = m(x − x1), m = f′(x1); normal: slope −1/m (if m = 0 the normal is x = x1; if the tangent is vertical the normal is y = y1).
  • Angle between two curves at a common point: tan θ = |(m1 − m2)/(1 + m1m2)|; orthogonal ⇔ m1m2 = −1.

ConceptMaxima and minima

  • First derivative test: f′ changes + to − at c: local max; − to +: local min; no change: neither (point of inflexion).
  • Second derivative test: f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0: local max; f″(c) > 0: local min; f″(c) = 0: the test fails — go back to the first derivative test (y = x4 has a minimum at 0 though f″(0) = 0).
  • Absolute extrema on [a, b]: compare f at the critical points inside and at the end points a, b.
  • Optimisation: write the quantity in one variable using the constraint, differentiate, confirm max/min with the sign of the second derivative, answer the question actually asked.

DiagramThe 2027 specimen roller coaster

DerivationEquations of tangent and normal

To prove. the tangent and normal to y = f(x) at P(x1, y1).

  1. The slope of the chord PQ with Q(x1 + h, f(x1 + h)) tends to f′(x1) as h → 0: the tangent’s slope is m = f′(x1).
  2. The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its slope m′ satisfies m m′ = −1.
tangent: y − y1 = f′(x1)(x − x1); normal: (y − y1)f′(x1) + (x − x1) = 0.

DerivationAngle between two curves

To prove. if the curves have tangent slopes m1, m2 at a common point, the acute angle θ between them satisfies tan θ = |(m1 − m2)/(1 + m1m2)|.

  1. The angle between curves is the angle between their tangents. Let the tangents make angles α, β with the x-axis: tan α = m1, tan β = m2.
  2. θ = |α − β| (or its supplement), and tan(α − β) = (tan α − tan β)/(1 + tan α tan β).
tan θ = |m1 − m21 + m1m2|; the curves cut orthogonally ⇔ m1m2 = −1.

Worked examples

Worked exampleAOD case study on a cubic (specimen 2027 Q17(i))

A1 D5

A roller-coaster track follows f(x) = x33 − 2x2 + 3x + 5, x ≥ 0. (a) Where is it rising, where falling? (b) Find the turning points. (c) Find the absolute max and min on [0, 4]. (d) The normal at x = 1.

Show working
  1. f′(x) = x2 − 4x + 3 = (x − 1)(x − 3).
  2. (a) f′ > 0 on [0, 1) and (3, ∞): rising; f′ < 0 on (1, 3): falling.
  3. (b) f(1) = ⅓ − 2 + 3 + 5 = 19/3 (local max), f(3) = 9 − 18 + 9 + 5 = 5 (local min).
  4. (c) f(0) = 5, f(4) = 64/3 − 32 + 12 + 5 = 19/3. Compare 5, 19/3, 5, 19/3.
  5. (d) f′(1) = 0: the tangent is horizontal, so the normal is vertical.

Answer turning points (1, 19/3) and (3, 5); on [0, 4] max 19/3, min 5; normal x = 1

Worked exampleDraining conical tank (specimen 2027 Q17(ii))

A2 D5

An inverted cone with semi-vertical angle tan−1(0·5) drains at 5 m3/min. How fast is the level falling when the water is 4 m deep?

Show working
  1. r/h = tan α = ½, so r = h/2 and V = ⅓π(h/2)2h = πh3/12.
  2. dV/dt = (πh2/4) dh/dt; at h = 4: −5 = 4π dh/dt.

Answer dh/dt = −54π m/min (falling at 5/(4π) m/min)

Worked exampleBalloon (B2026 Q6(i))

A3 B2

The surface of a spherical balloon grows at 4 cm2/s. How fast is its volume growing when r = 12 cm?

Show working
  1. S = 4πr2 ⇒ 8πr dr/dt = 4 ⇒ dr/dt = 1/(24π) at r = 12.
  2. dV/dt = 4πr2 dr/dt = 4π(144)/(24π).

Answer dV/dt = 24 cm3/s

Worked exampleA one-step rate (specimen 2027 Q1(iv) = NCERT Ex 6.1 Q11)

A4 A1

A particle moves on 6y = x3 + 2. Find the points where y changes 8 times as fast as x.

Show working
  1. 6 dy/dt = 3x2 dx/dt, and dy/dt = 8 dx/dt ⇒ x2 = 16.
  2. x = 4: y = 66/6 = 11; x = −4: y = −62/6.

Answer the points are (4, 11) and (−4, −31/3)

A5 B2

Show working
  1. f′(x) = 2xe−x − x2e−x = xe−x(2 − x).
  2. e−x > 0; x(2 − x) > 0 ⇔ 0 < x < 2.

Answer increasing on (0, 2), decreasing on (−∞, 0) and (2, ∞)

Worked exampleTangent parallel to a chord (B2024 Q4(ii) = specimen 2026 Q3)

A6 B2

Find the point on y = (x − 2)2 where the tangent is parallel to the chord joining (2, 0) and (4, 4).

Show working
  1. Chord slope = 4/2 = 2.
  2. y′ = 2(x − 2) = 2 ⇒ x = 3, y = 1.

Answer the point is (3, 1)

Worked exampleEquation of a normal (B2025I Q4)

A7 B2

Find the normal to y = x2 − 3x + 1 at (3, 1).

Show working
  1. y′ = 2x − 3 = 3 at x = 3; normal slope −1/3.
  2. y − 1 = −⅓(x − 3).

Answer normal: x + 3y = 6

Worked exampleCurves cutting orthogonally (specimen 2027 Q1(vi))

A8 A1

Find k if x = y2 and xy = k cut at right angles.

Show working
  1. At a common point x = y2, so y3 = k.
  2. Slopes: 1 = 2yy′ ⇒ m1 = 1/(2y); y + xy′ = 0 ⇒ m2 = −y/x = −1/y.
  3. m1m2 = −1/(2y2) = −1 ⇒ y2 = ½; k2 = y6 = ⅛.

Answer 8k2 = 1, k = ±1/(2√2)

Worked exampleCone of greatest volume in a sphere (B2018 Q12 = specimen 2021 Q13)

A9 D5

Show that the right circular cone of greatest volume inscribed in a sphere of radius R has height 4R/3. Find the height for R = 12 cm.

Show working
  1. With the centre O at distance x above the base: h = R + x, r2 = R2 − x2.
  2. V = ⅓π(R2 − x2)(R + x); dV/dx = ⅓π(R + x)(R − 3x).
  3. dV/dx = 0 ⇒ x = R/3; d2V/dx2 = ⅓π(−2R − 6x) < 0 there: a maximum.
  4. h = R + R/3 = 4R/3; Vmax = ⅓π(8R2/9)(4R/3) = 32πR3/81.

Answer h = 4R/3, Vmax = 32πR3/81; for R = 12 cm, h = 16 cm

Worked exampleCylinder in a sphere (specimen 2023 Q13(a))

A10 D5

Find the greatest volume of a cylinder inscribed in a sphere of radius 3√3 cm.

Show working
  1. Height h, radius r: r2 = 27 − h2/4; V = π(27h − h3/4).
  2. V′ = π(27 − 3h2/4) = 0 ⇒ h = 6; V″ = −3πh/2 < 0.
  3. r2 = 18, V = π(18)(6).

Answer h = 6 cm, r = 3√2 cm, Vmax = 108π cm3

Worked exampleLeast-cost box (B2019 Q12(a))

A11 D5

A closed box with a square base holds 4096 cm3. Find its dimensions for the least surface area.

Show working
  1. Base x, height 4096/x2: S = 2x2 + 4x(4096/x2) = 2x2 + 16384/x.
  2. S′ = 4x − 16384/x2 = 0 ⇒ x3 = 4096; S″ = 4 + 32768/x3 > 0.

Answer x = 16 cm, height 16 cm: a cube

Worked exampleNorman window (specimen 2022 Sem 1 Q22)

A12 D5

A window is a rectangle surmounted by a semicircle; its perimeter is 10 m. Find the radius for the greatest area.

Show working
  1. Width 2r, height y: 2r + 2y + πr = 10 ⇒ y = (10 − 2r − πr)/2.
  2. A = 2ry + πr2/2 = 10r − 2r2 − πr2/2.
  3. A′ = 10 − (4 + π)r = 0; A″ = −(4 + π) < 0.

Answer r = 104 + π m

Worked exampleAbsolute extrema on a closed interval (Heritage 2024 Q1(v))

A13 A1

Find the absolute maximum and minimum of f(x) = x4 + x + x2 on [−1, 1].

Show working
  1. f′(x) = (4 + x + x2) − x(1 + 2x)(4 + x + x2)2 = 4 − x2(…)2 > 0 on [−1, 1].
  2. So f is increasing: extremes at the end points. f(1) = 1/6, f(−1) = −1/4.

Answer maximum 1/6, minimum −1/4

Worked exampleLocal minimum by the first derivative (B2025 Q4(ii))

A14 B2

Find the minimum of f(x) = log(1 + x) + 11 + x, x > −1.

Show working
  1. f′(x) = 11 + x − 1(1 + x)2 = x(1 + x)2: negative for x < 0, positive for x > 0.

Answer minimum at x = 0, value 1

Worked exampleIncreasing for all x (specimen 2026 Q2(ii))

A15 B2

f(x) = b − ax + sin x is increasing on ℝ. Find the range of a.

Show working
  1. f′(x) = −a + cos x ≥ 0 for every x ⇔ −a ≥ 1 (the least value of cos x is −1).

Answer a ≤ −1

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Substituting the instant’s numbers before differentiating in a related-rates question.
  • Forgetting the end points when asked for the absolute maximum on [a, b].
  • Concluding “no extremum” because f″(c) = 0 (y = x4).
  • For a normal at a point where f′ = 0, writing slope −1/0 instead of the vertical line x = x1.
  • Maximising the wrong quantity: in A9 differentiate V, not r or h, and keep one variable.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • D5: an AOD case study on a cubic model (A1) or a related-rates cone (A2) — these are the two halves of the specimen’s Q17; boards set the same shape in 2025 and 2026 (ATMs at the turning points of 2x3 − 18x2 + 48x + 3).
  • D5 OR alternative: optimisation of a cone/cylinder in a sphere (A9, A10) or a box/window (A11, A12).
  • A1 (four of them): a rate of change (A4), increasing/decreasing from a context, angle between curves (A8), a local-extremum test (the second-derivative test failing).

6 · Integrals

Unit 3 · about 11 marks · three A1s, a 3-mark algebra-of-integrals, a 5-mark “hence” integral

ConceptMethods

  • Substitution: spot f′(x) beside a function of f(x). ∫f′(x)/f(x) dx = log|f(x)| + C; ∫f′(x)[f(x)]n dx = [f(x)]n+1/(n + 1) + C.
  • Parts: ∫u v dx = u∫v dx − ∫(u′∫v dx) dx. Choose u by ILATE (Inverse trig, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential).
  • Partial fractions (proper fraction): linear A/(x − a); repeated A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)2; quadratic (Ax + B)/(x2 + bx + c). Improper: divide first.
  • ex[f(x) + f′(x)] integrates to exf(x) + C: split the integrand to see f and f′.
  • (px + q)/(ax2 + bx + c): write px + q = A(2ax + b) + B; the A-part is a log, the B-part is a completed square.
  • Definite integrals: FTC ∫baf dx = F(b) − F(a); in a substitution change the limits too.

DerivationIntegration by parts

To prove. ∫uv dx = u∫v dx − ∫(u′∫v dx) dx.

  1. Let w = ∫v dx, so w′ = v. Product rule: (uw)′ = u′w + uw′ = u′w + uv.
  2. Integrate both sides: uw = ∫u′w dx + ∫uv dx.
∫uv dx = u∫v dx − ∫(u′∫v dx) dx; in particular ∫ex[f + f′] dx = exf + C.

Derivation∫ dx/(x2 − a2)

To prove. ∫1x2 − a2 dx = 12a log|x − ax + a| + C.

  1. 1x2 − a2 = 12a(1x − a − 1x + a) (partial fractions: 1 = A(x + a) + B(x − a), x = ±a).
  2. Integrate term by term: 12a[log|x − a| − log|x + a|].
12a log|x − ax + a| + C

Derivation∫ √(a2 − x2) dx

To prove. the formula in the sheet.

  1. By parts with u = √(a2 − x2), v = 1: I = x√(a2 − x2) + ∫x2√(a2 − x2) dx.
  2. Write x2 = a2 − (a2 − x2): the integral is a2 sin−1(x/a) − I.
  3. 2I = x√(a2 − x2) + a2 sin−1(x/a).
I = x2√(a2 − x2) + a22 sin−1xa + C.

DerivationThe properties of definite integrals

To prove. P0–P6 of the syllabus, from the FTC and a change of variable.

  1. P0 ∫baf(x) dx = ∫baf(t) dt: both are F(b) − F(a).
  2. P1 ∫baf = −∫abf: F(b) − F(a) = −[F(a) − F(b)].
  3. P2 ∫baf = ∫caf + ∫bcf: [F(c) − F(a)] + [F(b) − F(c)].
  4. P3 ∫baf(x) dx = ∫baf(a + b − x) dx: put t = a + b − x, dt = −dx; x = a ↔ t = b, x = b ↔ t = a; the integral becomes −∫abf(t) dt = ∫baf(t) dt by P1, then P0.
  5. P4 ∫a0f(x) dx = ∫a0f(a − x) dx: P3 with lower limit 0 and upper limit a, since 0 + a − x = a − x.
  6. P5 ∫2a0f = ∫a0f + ∫2aaf(x) dx; in the second put x = 2a − t: it becomes ∫a0f(2a − t) dt. So the total is 2∫a0f if f(2a − x) = f(x), and 0 if f(2a − x) = −f(x).
  7. P6 ∫a−af = ∫0−af(x) dx + ∫a0f; put x = −t in the first: it is ∫a0f(−t) dt. Even f: 2∫a0f; odd f: 0.
∫baf(x) dx = ∫baf(a + b − x) dx; ∫a−af = 2∫a0f (even), 0 (odd).

Caution P6 needs the whole integrand to be odd: x3 cos x is odd, x3 + cos x is neither.

DiagramWhy odd integrands vanish on [−a, a]

Worked examples — indefinite

Worked example“Hence” chained integral (specimen 2027 Q18(i))

I1 D5

(a) Find ∫log x dx. (b) Hence find ∫log[log((1 + x)/(1 − x))]1 − x2 dx, |x| < 1.

Show working
  1. (a) By parts, u = log x, v = 1: x log x − ∫x · (1/x) dx = x(log x − 1) + C.
  2. (b) t = log1 + x1 − x = log(1 + x) − log(1 − x), dt = (11 + x + 11 − x)dx = 21 − x2 dx.
  3. The integral is ½∫log t dt = ½ t(log t − 1) by (a).

Answer (a) x(log x − 1) + C; (b) ½ t(log t − 1) + C with t = log1 + x1 − x

Worked exampleThe same pattern, new data

I2 D5

Find ∫log(log x)x dx.

Show working
  1. t = log x, dt = dx/x: ∫log t dt = t(log t − 1).

Answer log x [log(log x) − 1] + C

Worked exampleRepeated linear and quadratic factors (B2025 Q11(ii))

I3 D5

Find ∫x2(x − 1)2(x2 + 1) dx.

Show working
  1. x2/[(x − 1)2(x2 + 1)] = A/(x − 1) + B/(x − 1)2 + (Cx + D)/(x2 + 1).
  2. x2 = A(x − 1)(x2 + 1) + B(x2 + 1) + (Cx + D)(x − 1)2; x = 1 gives B = ½.
  3. Compare coefficients: x3: A + C = 0; x: A + C − 2D = 0, so D = 0; constant: −A + B + D = 0, so A = ½, C = −½.
  4. Integrate: ½ log|x − 1| − 12(x − 1) − ¼ log(x2 + 1).

Answer ½ log|x − 1| − 12(x − 1) − ¼ log(x2 + 1) + C

Worked exampleSubstitution, then partial fractions (B2023 Q13(i))

I4 C3

Find ∫3e2x − 2exe2x + 2ex − 8 dx.

Show working
  1. t = ex, dt = exdx: ∫3t − 2(t + 4)(t − 2) dt.
  2. (3t − 2) = A(t − 2) + B(t + 4): t = 2 gives B = 4/6 = ⅔; t = −4 gives A = −14/−6 = 7/3.

Answer 73 log|ex + 4| + 23 log|ex − 2| + C

Worked exampleBy parts with an inverse trig function (B2025I Q9(i))

I5 B2

Find ∫x tan−1x dx.

Show working
  1. u = tan−1x, v = x: (x2/2) tan−1x − ½∫x21 + x2 dx.
  2. x2/(1 + x2) = 1 − 1/(1 + x2).

Answer x2 + 12 tan−1x − x2 + C

Worked exampleParts twice (B2025 Q8(ii))

I6 B2

Find ∫(log x)2 dx.

Show working
  1. u = (log x)2, v = 1: x(log x)2 − ∫2 log x dx.
  2. ∫log x dx = x log x − x.

Answer x(log x)2 − 2x log x + 2x + C

Worked exampleex[f + f′] (B2024 Q1(viii), specimen 2022)

I7 A1

Find (a) ∫ex(cot x − cosec2x) dx and (b) ∫ex x − 1x2 dx.

Show working
  1. (a) f = cot x, f′ = −cosec2x.
  2. (b) (x − 1)/x2 = 1/x − 1/x2: f = 1/x.

Answer (a) ex cot x + C; (b) ex/x + C

Worked exampleLinear over quadratic (B2024 Q9(ii))

I8 B2

Find ∫x + 7x2 + 4x + 7 dx.

Show working
  1. x + 7 = ½(2x + 4) + 5.
  2. ½∫2x + 4x2 + 4x + 7 dx = ½ log(x2 + 4x + 7).
  3. 5∫1(x + 2)2 + 3 dx = 5√3 tan−1x + 2√3.

Answer ½ log(x2 + 4x + 7) + 5√3 tan−1x + 2√3 + C

Worked exampleComplete the square under a root (B2020 Q8(a))

I9 B2

Find ∫1√(5x − 4x2) dx.

Show working
  1. 5x − 4x2 = 4[(5/8)2 − (x − 5/8)2].
  2. So the integral is ½ sin−1x − 5/85/8.

Answer ½ sin−18x − 55 + C

Worked exampleA trigonometric quadratic (B2025I Q9(ii))

I10 B2

Find ∫cos xsin2x + 4 sin x + 5 dx.

Show working
  1. t = sin x: ∫1(t + 2)2 + 1 dt.

Answer tan−1(sin x + 2) + C

Worked example∫ dx/(a + b cos x) (syllabus type)

I11 C3

Find ∫15 + 4 cos x dx.

Show working
  1. t = tan(x/2): cos x = (1 − t2)/(1 + t2), dx = 2dt/(1 + t2).
  2. Denominator 5(1 + t2) + 4(1 − t2) = 9 + t2: ∫29 + t2 dt = ⅔ tan−1(t/3).

Answer 23 tan−1(13 tan x2) + C

Worked example∫ √(ax2 + bx + c) (syllabus type, not yet set)

I12 C3

Find ∫√(x2 + 4x + 8) dx.

Show working
  1. x2 + 4x + 8 = (x + 2)2 + 22; use the √(u2 + a2) formula with u = x + 2, a = 2.

Answer x + 22√(x2 + 4x + 8) + 2 log|x + 2 + √(x2 + 4x + 8)| + C

Worked exampleWhich answers are right? (specimen 2027 Q1(x) format)

I13 A1

Three students give ∫sin 2x dx as (i) −½ cos 2x + C, (ii) sin2x + C, (iii) −cos2x + C. Which are correct?

Show working
  1. Differentiate each: (i) sin 2x; (ii) 2 sin x cos x = sin 2x; (iii) 2 cos x sin x = sin 2x.
  2. They differ by constants: sin2x = ½ − ½ cos 2x, −cos2x = −½ − ½ cos 2x.

Answer all three are correct

Worked examples — definite

Worked exampleAlgebra of definite integrals (specimen 2027 Q14)

I14 C3

Given ∫513f(x) dx = 12, find ∫15f(x) dx and ∫21(x + f(x)) dx + ∫52(x + f(x)) dx.

Show working
  1. ∫51f = 4, so ∫15f = −4 (P1).
  2. By P2 the sum is ∫51(x + f(x)) dx = [x2/2]15 + 4 = 12 + 4.

Answer ∫15f = −4; the sum is 16

Worked exampleKing’s property (specimen 2026 Q5(ii))

I15 B2

Evaluate ∫50√x√(5 − x) + √x dx.

Show working
  1. By P4, I = ∫50√(5 − x)√x + √(5 − x) dx.
  2. Add: 2I = ∫501 dx = 5.

Answer I = 5/2

Worked examplex f(sin x): remove the x (B2025 Q11(i) = specimen 2026 Q12(ii))

I16 C3

Evaluate ∫3π/4π/4x1 + sin x dx.

Show working
  1. P3: a + b − x = π − x and sin(π − x) = sin x, so I = ∫3π/4π/4π − x1 + sin x dx.
  2. 2I = π∫3π/4π/411 + sin x dx = π∫3π/4π/41 − sin xcos2x dx = π[tan x − sec x]π/43π/4.
  3. [tan x − sec x] = (−1 + √2) − (1 − √2) = 2√2 − 2.

Answer I = (√2 − 1)π

Worked exampleThe 1/(1 + eg) property (B2024 Q5)

I17 B2

Evaluate ∫2π011 + esin x dx.

Show working
  1. P4 with a = 2π: sin(2π − x) = −sin x, and 11 + e−s = eses + 1.
  2. Adding, the integrand becomes 1: 2I = 2π.

Answer I = π

Worked exampleModulus integral (specimen 2023 Q9(a))

I18 C3

Evaluate ∫2−1|x3 − x| dx.

Show working
  1. x3 − x = x(x − 1)(x + 1): ≥ 0 on [−1, 0], ≤ 0 on [0, 1], ≥ 0 on [1, 2].
  2. F = x4/4 − x2/2: pieces ¼ + ¼ + (2 + ¼).

Answer value 11/4

Worked exampleGreatest integer (specimen 2025 Q3)

I19 B2

Evaluate ∫√20[x2] dx.

Show working
  1. [x2] = 0 on [0, 1) and 1 on [1, √2).

Answer value √2 − 1

Worked exampleA log integral by P4 (B2017 Q1(vi))

I20 C3

Evaluate ∫π/40log(1 + tan x) dx.

Show working
  1. P4: 1 + tan(π/4 − x) = 1 + 1 − tan x1 + tan x = 21 + tan x.
  2. So I = ∫π/40[log 2 − log(1 + tan x)] dx = (π/4) log 2 − I.

Answer I = (π/8) log 2

Worked exampleOdd-function A–R (specimen 2027 Q1(xvii))

I21 A1

Assertion: ∫1−1x3 cos x dx = 0. Reason: ∫a0f(x) dx = ∫a0f(a − x) dx.

Show working
  1. x3 cos x is odd, so the assertion is true (by P6).
  2. The reason is a true property (P4) but it is not what makes the assertion true.

Answer the integral is 0: A and R both true, R not the reason — option (b)

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Changing the variable in a definite integral but keeping the old limits.
  • Using P6 on an integrand that is neither odd nor even.
  • Omitting + C, or writing log(x − 1) without the modulus.
  • Partial fractions on an improper fraction without dividing first.
  • In a modulus integral, splitting at the wrong points: find the zeros of the expression inside inside the interval.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • D5 “hence” integral: (a) a standard integral such as ∫log x dx or ∫tan x dx; (b) a substitution that reduces a harder one to (a) (I1, I2). Exactly the 2027 specimen shape.
  • C3: the algebra of definite integrals from given values (I14) — new in the 2027 specimen; or x f(sin x) / King’s property (I15, I16).
  • A1 (three): odd/even A–R (I21), an error-analysis MCQ on an antiderivative (I13), a direct FTC evaluation or an ex(f + f′) (I7).
  • Partial fractions with a repeated or quadratic factor (I3) and substitution-then-partial-fractions (I4) remain the most-set board integrals.

7 · Area under Curves

Unit 3 · about 4 marks · a 1-mark “which integral gives the shaded area” and a 3-mark area between curves

ConceptSetting up an area

  • Area between y = f(x) ≥ g(x) from a to b: ∫ba[f(x) − g(x)] dx (top minus bottom). With horizontal strips: ∫dc[xright − xleft] dy.
  • Always sketch, find the intersection points, and decide top and bottom from the sketch.
  • Where a curve crosses the axis, split the interval: the area is ∫ba|f| dx, not ∫baf dx.
  • Symmetry halves the work: y2 = 4ax is symmetric in the x-axis, a circle in both axes.

DerivationArea of a circle and an ellipse

To prove. the circle x2 + y2 = a2 has area πa2; the ellipse x2/a2 + y2/b2 = 1 has area πab.

  1. By symmetry the circle’s area is 4∫a0√(a2 − x2) dx.
  2. By the formula sheet, [x2√(a2 − x2) + a22 sin−1xa]0a = a22 · π2.
  3. For the ellipse y = (b/a)√(a2 − x2), so the area is (b/a) times the circle’s.
circle πa2; ellipse πab.

y2 = 4ax and x = a8a2/3
y2 = 4ax and x2 = 4ay16a2/3
Circle, ellipseπa2, πab

Worked examples

Worked exampleParabola and line through two points (specimen 2027 Q15(ii))

Ar1 C3

The line y = −3x + 9 meets the axes at P and Q. The parabola y = ax2 + c passes through P and Q. Find the parabola and the area between it and the line.

Show working
  1. P = (0, 9), Q = (3, 0). Through P: c = 9; through Q: 9a + 9 = 0, a = −1: y = 9 − x2.
  2. On [0, 3] the parabola is on top: ∫30[(9 − x2) − (9 − 3x)] dx = [3x2/2 − x3/3]03 = 27/2 − 9.

Answer y = 9 − x2; area 9/2 sq units

Worked exampleTwo parabolas (B2024 Q18(ii))

Ar2 C3

Find the area between y2 = 4x and x2 = 4y.

Show working
  1. They meet at (0, 0) and (4, 4).
  2. ∫40(2√x − x2/4) dx = [⁴⁄₃ x3/2 − x3/12]04 = 32/3 − 16/3.

Answer area 16/3 sq units

Worked exampleSketch, then hence (specimen 2026 Q18)

Ar3 C3

Find the area bounded by y = x(4 − x), the x-axis, and x = 0 to x = 5.

Show working
  1. The curve is below the axis on (4, 5): split at 4.
  2. ∫40(4x − x2) dx = 32 − 64/3 = 32/3; |∫54(4x − x2) dx| = |(50 − 125/3) − 32/3| = 7/3.

Answer area = 32/3 + 7/3 = 13 sq units (not ∫50f = 25/3)

Worked exampleWhich integral gives the shaded area? (specimen 2027 Q1(viii))

Ar4 A1

Write the area bounded by x + 2y = 8, x = 2 and the x-axis, shaded below, as an integral and evaluate it.

Show working
  1. The line meets the x-axis at x = 8; y = 4 − x/2 ≥ 0 on [2, 8].
  2. A triangle with base 6 and height 3: a check on the integral.

Answer area = ∫82(4 − x/2) dx = 9 sq units

Worked exampleArea with a modulus (B2018 Q17(b) = specimen 2021 Q18)

Ar5 B2

Find the area under y = |x + 4| from x = −6 to x = 0.

Show working
  1. Split at x = −4: ∫−4−6−(x + 4) dx + ∫0−4(x + 4) dx = 2 + 8.

Answer area 10 sq units

Worked exampleFind the parameter (specimen 2023 Q18)

Ar6 C3

The area between y2 = 16x and y = 4mx (m > 0) is 1/12. Find m.

Show working
  1. Intersections: 16m2x2 = 16x ⇒ x = 0, 1/m2.
  2. Area = ∫1/m20(4√x − 4mx) dx = 8/(3m3) − 2/m3 = 2/(3m3) = 1/12.

Answer m3 = 8, m = 2

Worked exampleExponential and log curves (syllabus line, not yet set)

Ar7 B2

Find the area under y = ex from x = 0 to 1, and under y = log x from x = 1 to e.

Show working
  1. ∫10ex dx = e − 1.
  2. ∫e1log x dx = [x log x − x]1e = 0 − (−1).

Answer areas e − 1 and 1 sq units

Worked exampleA semicircle (B2026 Q18)

Ar8 B2

Find the area bounded by y = √(4 − x2) and the x-axis.

Show working
  1. ∫2−2√(4 − x2) dx = 2∫20√(4 − x2) dx = 2 · (4/2)(π/2).

Answer area 2π sq units

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Integrating f from a to b across a zero and reporting a signed value (Ar3).
  • Subtracting bottom minus top and getting a negative area.
  • Not finding the intersection points first: the limits come from them.
  • Drawing no sketch: in ISC the sketch carries a mark.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • C3: parabola–line (Ar1) or two parabolas (Ar2), often scaffolded “(a) find the curve, (b) hence the area”.
  • A1: choose the integral that gives a shaded area (Ar4) — new in the 2027 specimen.
  • Also due: an area under ex or log x (Ar7), listed in the syllabus but never yet set.

8 · Differential Equations

Unit 3 · 3–6 marks · a 1-mark order/degree or separable item and a 2-mark homogeneous or linear equation

ConceptDefinitions

  • Order: the highest derivative present. Degree: the power of that derivative once the equation is a polynomial in the derivatives (undefined if a derivative sits inside log, sin, e( ), etc.).
  • The general solution has as many arbitrary constants as the order; a particular solution fixes them from given conditions.
  • Forming a DE: differentiate as many times as there are constants, then eliminate them.
  • Second-order equations are not solved in ISC 2027 (showing that a given y satisfies one is differentiation, Unit 4).

ConceptThe three solvable types

TypeRecogniseMethod
Variable separabledy/dx = g(x)h(y)∫dy/h(y) = ∫g(x) dx; reducible ones by x + y = v
Homogeneousdy/dx = F(y/x) (every term of the same degree)y = vx, dy/dx = v + x dv/dx; or x = vy for dx/dy = F(x/y)
Linear in ydy/dx + Py = Q, P, Q functions of xIF = e∫P dx; y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C
Linear in xdx/dy + Px = Q, P, Q functions of yIF = e∫P dy; x·IF = ∫Q·IF dy + C

DerivationThe integrating factor

To prove. dy/dx + Py = Q has solution y e∫P dx = ∫Q e∫P dx dx + C.

  1. Let R = e∫P dx, so R′ = PR.
  2. Multiply the equation by R: Ry′ + PRy = QR, i.e. Ry′ + R′y = QR.
  3. The left side is (Ry)′; integrate both sides.
y · IF = ∫Q · IF dx + C, with IF = e∫P dx.

Caution e∫P with ∫P = log|f| gives IF = |f| — drop the modulus only when f keeps one sign on the interval.

DerivationWhy y = vx works for a homogeneous equation

To prove. dy/dx = F(y/x) separates under y = vx.

  1. y = vx ⇒ dy/dx = v + x dv/dx.
  2. So v + x dv/dx = F(v), i.e. dvF(v) − v = dxx: separable.
∫dvF(v) − v = log|x| + C, then put v = y/x back.

DiagramA family of solution curves

FormulaeDifferential equations at a glance

ResultFormulaNote
Separabledy/dx = g(x)h(y) ⇒ ∫dy/h(y) = ∫g(x) dx
Homogeneousy = vx: v + x dv/dx = F(v)x = vy for dx/dy = F(x/y)
Linear in yy e∫P dx = ∫Q e∫P dx dx + C
Linear in xx e∫P dy = ∫Q e∫P dy dy + C
Common IFs∫P = log x ⇒ IF = x; ∫P = −log x ⇒ IF = 1/x; P = 1/(1 + x2) ⇒ IF = etan−1x
Growth/decaydN/dt = kN ⇒ N = N0ektdoubling time (log 2)/k

Worked examples

Worked exampleOrder and degree (specimen 2023 Q1(ix), S2021 Q1(xiii))

E1 A1

State the order and degree of (a) y″ + 3(y′)2 = x2 log(y″); (b) (y′)5 + 3xy(y‴)2 + y2(y″)3 = 0, and the sum for (b).

Show working
  1. (a) y″ is inside a log: order 2, degree not defined.
  2. (b) highest derivative y‴, raised to the power 2: order 3, degree 2.

Answer (a) order 2, degree undefined; (b) order 3, degree 2, sum 5

Worked exampleA separable equation that is a circle (specimen 2027 Q1(xix))

E2 A1

The solution of dydx = ax + 32y + 5 is a family of circles. Find a.

Show working
  1. Separate: (2y + 5)dy = (ax + 3)dx ⇒ y2 + 5y = ax2/2 + 3x + C.
  2. A circle needs the x2 and y2 coefficients equal on the same side: −a/2 = 1.

Answer a = −2

Worked exampleSeparable with a condition (B2024 Q13(ii))

E3 B2

Solve x(x2 − 1) dy/dx = 1, given y = 0 when x = 2.

Show working
  1. dy = dx/[x(x − 1)(x + 1)] = [−1/x + ½/(x − 1) + ½/(x + 1)]dx.
  2. y = ½ log|x2 − 1| − log|x| + C; at x = 2: 0 = ½ log 3 − log 2 + C.

Answer y = ½ log|x2 − 1x2| − ½ log 34

Worked exampleHomogeneous (B2023 Q10(ii))

E4 B2

Solve (x2 − y2)dx + 2xy dy = 0.

Show working
  1. dy/dx = (y2 − x2)/(2xy). y = vx: v + xv′ = (v2 − 1)/(2v) ⇒ xv′ = −(1 + v2)/(2v).
  2. 2v1 + v2dv = −dxx ⇒ log(1 + v2) = −log|x| + log c ⇒ x(1 + y2/x2) = c.

Answer x2 + y2 = cx

Worked exampleHomogeneous with a condition (B2025 Q12(ii))

E5 B2

Solve (x2 − 2y2)dx + 2xy dy = 0, y(1) = 1.

Show working
  1. dy/dx = (2y2 − x2)/(2xy); y = vx: xv′ = −1/(2v) ⇒ 2v dv = −dx/x.
  2. v2 = −log|x| + C; at (1, 1): C = 1.

Answer y2 = x2(1 − log|x|)

Worked exampledx/dy = x/y + f(x/y)/f′(x/y) (specimen 2027 Q4)

E6 B2

Solve the equation and show f(x/y) = cy.

Show working
  1. x = vy: dx/dy = v + y dv/dy, so y dv/dy = f(v)/f′(v).
  2. f′(v)dv/f(v) = dy/y ⇒ log|f(v)| = log|y| + log|c|.

Answer f(x/y) = cy

Worked exampleLinear in y (specimen 2026 Q9(ii), B2020 Q9)

E7 B2

Solve (1 + x2) dy/dx + 2xy = 4x2.

Show working
  1. Here the left side is already d/dx[(1 + x2)y] (IF = 1 + x2 after dividing by it).
  2. Integrate: (1 + x2)y = 4x3/3 + C.

Answer y(1 + x2) = 4x33 + C

Worked exampleLinear with an ITF (specimen 2023 Q12(a))

E8 C3

Solve (1 + x2)dy = (tan−1x − y)dx, y(0) = 1.

Show working
  1. dy/dx + y/(1 + x2) = tan−1x/(1 + x2); IF = etan−1x.
  2. With t = tan−1x: yet = ∫tet dt = (t − 1)et + C.
  3. y(0) = 1: 1 = −1 + C, C = 2.

Answer y = tan−1x − 1 + 2e−tan−1x

Worked exampleLinear in x (B2026 Q14(ii))

E9 C3

Solve √(1 − y2) dx = (sin−1y − x) dy, x = 0 when y = 0.

Show working
  1. dx/dy + x/√(1 − y2) = sin−1y/√(1 − y2); IF = esin−1y.
  2. x es = (s − 1)es + C with s = sin−1y; at (0, 0): C = 1.

Answer x = sin−1y − 1 + e−sin−1y

Worked exampleForm the DE (B2020 Q1(viii), S2018 Q1(vii))

E10 A1

Eliminate the constants: (a) y = Aex + Be−x; (b) y2 = 4ax.

Show working
  1. (a) y′ = Aex − Be−x, y″ = Aex + Be−x = y.
  2. (b) 2yy′ = 4a = y2/x.

Answer (a) y″ = y; (b) 2xy′ = y

Worked exampleGrowth model (B2018 Q9(b))

E11 B2

A population grows at 10% of itself per year. How long does it take to become four times as large?

Show working
  1. dP/dt = 0·1P ⇒ P = P0e0·1t.
  2. 4 = e0·1t ⇒ t = 10 log 4.

Answer t = 10 log 4 ≈ 13·9 years

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Calling the degree 1 when a derivative sits inside a log (E1).
  • In a linear equation, not first dividing so that the coefficient of dy/dx is 1 before reading off P.
  • Forgetting the constant of integration before applying the initial condition.
  • Using y = vx on an equation in dx/dy form (x/y): use x = vy there (E6).

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • B2: a homogeneous equation (E4, E5, E6) or a linear equation (E7–E9) — in every recent board; 2027 specimen Q4 was the x = vy form.
  • A1: order and degree (E1) or “the solution is a circle” (E2).
  • Specimen 2027 gave DE only 3 marks, against 7 in every recent board: a 3-mark linear equation with a condition (E8, E9) is quite possible.

9 · Vectors

Unit 4 · 5 marks · one A1 and two 2-mark questions, one of them an application on a map or a solid

ConceptVector basics

  • A vector has magnitude and direction; a = a1î + a2ĵ + a3k̂, |a| = √(a12 + a22 + a32), unit vector â = a/|a|.
  • Direction cosines of a: (a1, a2, a3)/|a|; l2 + m2 + n2 = 1. Direction ratios are any multiple.
  • Position vector of P dividing AB in m : n internally: (mb + na)/(m + n); externally (mb − na)/(m − n).
  • a and b are collinear (parallel) ⇔ b = λa ⇔ a × b = 0. Three points are collinear ⇔ AB and BC are parallel.

ConceptDot and cross products

  • a·b = |a||b| cos θ = a1b1 + a2b2 + a3b3; perpendicular ⇔ a·b = 0; obtuse ⇔ a·b < 0 (and not antiparallel).
  • Scalar projection of b on a: a·b/|a|; vector projection: (a·b/|a|2)a.
  • a × b = |a||b| sin θ n̂, perpendicular to both; b × a = −a × b; î × ĵ = k̂ (cyclic).
  • Area of the parallelogram on a, b = |a × b|; of a triangle ABC = ½|AB × AC|; with diagonals d1, d2, parallelogram = ½|d1 × d2|.
  • Not in 2027: the scalar triple product and proofs of geometrical theorems by vectors.

DiagramAdding vectors

The two laws give the same sum: the diagonal of the parallelogram is the third side of the triangle.

DiagramProjection and area

DerivationProjection formula

To prove. the scalar projection of b on a is a·b/|a|.

  1. From the figure the projection is |b| cos θ.
  2. cos θ = a·b/(|a||b|).
scalar projection = a·b|a|; vector projection = a·b|a|2 a.

Caution the projection is signed: a negative value means the angle is obtuse.

Derivation|a × b|2 + (a·b)2 = |a|2|b|2

To prove. the identity that turns dot data into cross data.

  1. |a × b|2 = |a|2|b|2 sin2θ, (a·b)2 = |a|2|b|2 cos2θ.
  2. Add.
|a × b|2 + (a·b)2 = |a|2|b|2; so |a × b| = a·b ⇔ θ = π/4.

FormulaeVectors at a glance

ResultFormulaNote
|a ± b|2|a|2 + |b|2 ± 2a·ba ⊥ b: Pythagoras
(a + b)·(a − b)|a|2 − |b|2
Anglecos θ = a·b/(|a||b|)
Unit normal to a, b±(a × b)/|a × b|
Cross productîĵk̂a1a2a3b1b2b3expand along row 1
Triangle area½|AB × AC|

Worked examples

Worked exampleScalar and vector projection (specimen 2027 Q7(i))

V1 B2

Find the scalar and vector projections of B = 6î + 3ĵ + 2k̂ on A = î − 2ĵ − 2k̂.

Show working
  1. A·B = 6 − 6 − 4 = −4, |A| = 3.

Answer scalar projection −4/3; vector projection −(4/9)(î − 2ĵ − 2k̂)

Worked exampleUnit vector perpendicular to a plane through three points (specimen 2027 Q7(ii))

V2 B2

A(1, 1, 1), B(2, 3, −4), C(7, 4, 9). Find a unit vector perpendicular to the plane ABC.

Show working
  1. AB = î + 2ĵ − 5k̂, AC = 6î + 3ĵ + 8k̂.
  2. AB × AC = (16 + 15)î − (8 + 30)ĵ + (3 − 12)k̂ = 31î − 38ĵ − 9k̂.
  3. |AB × AC|2 = 961 + 1444 + 81 = 2486.

Answer ±(31î − 38ĵ − 9k̂)/√2486

Worked exampleVectors on a map (specimen 2027 Q8)

V3 B2

On a map with O as origin, IMA is at I = 3î + 9ĵ and Rajpur at R = 8î + 4ĵ. The bus stop S is ⅔ of the way from O to I. Show that S is the point of OI nearest to R.

Show working
  1. S = ⅔(3î + 9ĵ) = 2î + 6ĵ.
  2. RS = S − R = −6î + 2ĵ.
  3. OS·RS = 2(−6) + 6(2) = 0, so RS ⊥ OI: the perpendicular from R meets OI at S, the nearest point.

Answer S = 2î + 6ĵ, OS·RS = 0

Worked example|a + b| with a ⊥ b (B2026, S2021, B2019 — set three times)

V4 A1

a ⊥ b, |a + b| = 13, |a| = 5. Find |b|.
Show working
  1. |a + b|2 = |a|2 + |b|2 since a·b = 0: 169 = 25 + |b|2.

Answer |b| = 12

Worked exampleParallelogram from its diagonals (B2023 Q15(iii))

V5 B2

The diagonals of a parallelogram are î − 3ĵ + k̂ and î + ĵ + k̂. Find its area.

Show working
  1. d1 × d2 = (−3 − 1)î − (1 − 1)ĵ + (1 + 3)k̂ = −4î + 4k̂.
  2. Area = ½|d1 × d2| = ½ · 4√2.

Answer area 2√2 sq units

Worked exampleObtuse angle condition (specimens 2025, 2026 Q16(ii))

V6 B2

Find x for which 2x2î + 3xĵ + k̂ and î − 2ĵ + x2k̂ make an obtuse angle.

Show working
  1. Dot product 2x2 − 6x + x2 = 3x(x − 2) < 0 ⇔ 0 < x < 2.
  2. The vectors are never antiparallel (their k-components are both positive), so no value is excluded.

Answer 0 < x < 2

V7 B2

Find a vector of magnitude 9 perpendicular to 4î − ĵ + k̂ and −2î + ĵ − 2k̂.

Show working
  1. Cross product: (2 − 1)î − (−8 + 2)ĵ + (4 − 2)k̂ = î + 6ĵ + 2k̂, magnitude √41.

Answer ±(9/√41)(î + 6ĵ + 2k̂)

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Dividing by |b| instead of |a| in the projection of b on a.
  • Giving one unit normal: there are two, ±.
  • Using a·b < 0 as the whole obtuse condition without checking for θ = π.
  • Forgetting the ½ for a triangle or for a parallelogram given by its diagonals.
  • Sign slips in the middle term of a cross product: it is −(a1b3 − a3b1).

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • B2 application: position vectors on a map or a solid, with a perpendicularity or nearest-point check (V3).
  • B2: projection (V1) or a unit vector perpendicular to a plane (V2, V7).
  • A1: a cross/dot numeric (V8), |a + b| (V4), collinearity (V9).

10 · Three-dimensional Geometry

Unit 5 · 6 marks · an A1 on lines meeting or DCs, a 2-mark angle, a 3-mark plane/line question

ConceptLines

  • Through A(a) parallel to b: r = a + λb; Cartesian (x − x1)/a = (y − y1)/b = (z − z1)/c.
  • Through two points: direction ratios (x2 − x1, y2 − y1, z2 − z1). Put every coefficient of x, y, z to +1 before reading ratios (2x − 3 = 3y + 1 = 5 − 6z has ratios (1/2, 1/3, −1/6)).
  • Angle between lines: cos θ = |b1·b2|/(|b1||b2|); perpendicular a1a2 + b1b2 + c1c2 = 0; parallel: ratios proportional.
  • Two lines intersect if the general points can be made equal; skew if they are neither parallel nor intersecting. Coplanar ⇔ (a2 − a1)·(b1 × b2) = 0.
  • Axes: x-axis y = 0, z = 0 (r = λî); the xy-plane is z = 0.

ConceptPlanes

  • Normal form r·n̂ = d (d = distance from O); Cartesian ax + by + cz + d = 0 with normal (a, b, c).
  • Through a point with normal n: (r − a)·n = 0. Intercept form x/a + y/b + z/c = 1.
  • Through three points: normal AB × AC. Perpendicular to two planes: normal n1 × n2.
  • Angle between planes = angle between normals; between a line (b) and a plane (n): sin φ = |b·n|/(|b||n|).
  • Distance of (x1, y1, z1) from ax + by + cz + d = 0: |ax1 + by1 + cz1 + d|/√(a2 + b2 + c2).
  • Not in 2027: the family of planes through the intersection of two planes; image of a line in a plane.

DiagramPoint, plane, line: the three pictures

DerivationDistance of a point from a plane

To prove. the distance of P(x1, y1, z1) from ax + by + cz + d = 0 is |ax1 + by1 + cz1 + d|/√(a2 + b2 + c2).

  1. Take any point A(x0, y0, z0) on the plane, so ax0 + by0 + cz0 = −d.
  2. The distance PN is the length of the projection of AP on the normal n = (a, b, c): |AP·n|/|n|.
  3. AP·n = a(x1 − x0) + b(y1 − y0) + c(z1 − z0) = ax1 + by1 + cz1 + d.
PN = |ax1 + by1 + cz1 + d|√(a2 + b2 + c2); for parallel planes ax + by + cz + di = 0 the gap is |d1 − d2|/√(a2 + b2 + c2).

DerivationShortest distance between skew lines

To prove. for r = a1 + λb1 and r = a2 + μb2, SD = |(a2 − a1)·(b1 × b2)|/|b1 × b2|.

  1. The common perpendicular PQ is perpendicular to both b1 and b2, so it lies along b1 × b2.
  2. A1(a1) and A2(a2) are points on the two lines; PQ is the projection of A1A2 on that direction.
SD = |(a2 − a1)·(b1 × b2)||b1 × b2|; parallel lines (b1 = b2 = b): SD = |b × (a2 − a1)|/|b|.

Caution SD = 0 means the lines intersect (they are coplanar).

DerivationDistance of a point from a line

To prove. the distance of P from the line r = a + λb.

  1. A general point of the line is Q(a + λb).
  2. Q is the foot of the perpendicular ⇔ PQ·b = 0: this linear equation gives λ.
  3. The distance is |PQ| for that λ; the image of P in the line is 2Q − P.
distance = |PQ| with (a + λb − p)·b = 0; equivalently |b × (p − a)|/|b|.

Formulae3-D geometry at a glance

Equal DCs(±1/√3, ±1/√3, ±1/√3)(1, 1, 1) are not DCs
Plane, 3 pointsx − x1y − y1z − z1x2 − x1y2 − y1z2 − z1x3 − x1y3 − y1z3 − z1 = 0
Angle of planescos θ = |n1·n2|/(|n1||n2|)
Line and planesin φ = |b·n|/(|b||n|)parallel ⇔ b·n = 0

Skew lines|(a2 − a1)·(b1 × b2)|/|b1 × b2|

G5 C3

Balloons follow (x − 1)/2 = (y − b)/3 = (z − 3)/4 and (x − 4)/5 = (y − 1)/2 = z/1. For which b do the paths meet, and where?

G6 C3

A microphone is at M(3, 2, 1) and a wall is 2x − y + z + 1 = 0. Find the distance of M from the wall and the image of M in it.

Show working
  1. Distance |6 − 2 + 1 + 1|/√6 = 6/√6.
  2. Foot: (3, 2, 1) − (6/6)(2, −1, 1) = (1, 3, 0); image = 2 · foot − M.

Answer distance √6; image (−1, 4, −1)

Worked exampleAngle between planes (B2025 Q15(ii))

G7 A1

Find the angle between x + y + 2z = 9 and 2x − y + z = 15.

Show working
  1. cos θ = (2 − 1 + 2)/(√6 · √6) = ½.

Answer θ = π/3

Worked examplePlane through three points (B2025 Q16(i))

G8 B2

Find the plane through (2, 2, −1), (3, 4, 2), (7, 0, 6).

Show working
  1. AB = (1, 2, 3), AC = (5, −2, 7); AB × AC = (14 + 6, −(7 − 15), −2 − 10) = (20, 8, −12) ∝ (5, 2, −3).
  2. 5(2) + 2(2) − 3(−1) = 17.

Answer 5x + 2y − 3z = 17

Worked examplePlane perpendicular to two planes (B2023 Q17(i))

G9 C3

Find the plane through (1, 1, −1) perpendicular to x + 2y + 3z = 7 and 2x − 3y + 4z = 0.

Show working
  1. Normal = (1, 2, 3) × (2, −3, 4) = (8 + 9, 6 − 4, −3 − 4) = (17, 2, −7).
  2. 17 + 2 + 7 = 26.

Answer 17x + 2y − 7z = 26

Worked exampleLine perpendicular to two lines (B2019 Q17(b) = specimen 2021 Q17(b))

G10 C3

Find the line through (2, 1, 3) perpendicular to (x − 1)/1 = (y − 2)/2 = (z − 3)/3 and x/(−3) = y/2 = z/5.

Show working
  1. Direction = (1, 2, 3) × (−3, 2, 5) = (10 − 6, −9 − 5, 2 + 6) = (4, −14, 8) ∝ (2, −7, 4).

Answer (x − 2)/2 = (y − 1)/(−7) = (z − 3)/4

Worked exampleFoot, image and distance from a line (Exemplar Ch 11 Ex 12)

G11 C3

Find the foot of the perpendicular from P(1, 6, 3) to x/1 = (y − 1)/2 = (z − 2)/3, the image of P, and the distance.

Show working
  1. General point Q(t, 1 + 2t, 2 + 3t); PQ = (t − 1, 2t − 5, 3t − 1).
  2. PQ·(1, 2, 3) = 14t − 14 = 0 ⇒ t = 1, Q = (1, 3, 5).
  3. Image 2Q − P; distance |PQ| = √(0 + 9 + 4).

Answer foot (1, 3, 5), image (1, 0, 7), distance √13

Worked exampleDirection cosines (B2026 Q15(iii))

G12 A1

Find the direction cosines of the line through P(2, 3, 5) and Q(−1, 2, 4).

Show working
  1. PQ has ratios (−3, −1, −1) ∝ (3, 1, 1); magnitude √11.

Answer DCs ±(3, 1, 1)/√11

Worked exampleEqual intercepts (B2023 Q15(iv))

G13 A1

Find the plane with equal intercepts through (2, 4, 6).

Show working
  1. x/a + y/a + z/a = 1 ⇒ x + y + z = a = 2 + 4 + 6.

Answer x + y + z = 12

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Reading direction ratios off a line whose x, y, z have coefficients other than 1 (put each in the form (x − α)/l).
  • Using cos instead of sin for the angle between a line and a plane.
  • Forgetting the modulus in the distance formula, or the √ in the denominator.
  • Taking a negative cos γ when the question says the angle is acute (G1).
  • Declaring lines skew without checking parallelism first.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • C3: a line–plane intersection chain (G2) or a plane from its normal (G1) — the two halves of specimen Q12; also a plane through three points or perpendicular to two planes (G8, G9).
  • B2: the angle between a line and a plane (G3), between two planes (G7).
  • A1: two lines meeting (G5, specimen 2027 Q1(xii)), direction cosines (G12), intercepts (G13).
  • Under-examined syllabus lines that are due: shortest distance between skew lines (G4) and distance of a point from a line (G11).

11 · Linear Programming

Unit 6 · 5 marks · two A1s (theory, equal optima at two corners) and a 3-mark graphical problem

ConceptTerminology and method

  • Decision variables x, y ≥ 0; constraints (linear inequalities); objective function Z = px + qy to maximise or minimise.
  • The feasible region is the intersection of the half-planes; any point in it is a feasible solution; if it is empty the problem is infeasible.
  • Corner point theorem: if an optimum exists, it occurs at a corner of the feasible region. If Z has the same optimal value at two adjacent corners, every point of the edge joining them is optimal (infinitely many optima).
  • Unbounded region: the corner value may not be the optimum. To confirm a maximum M, check that the open half-plane px + qy > M has no point in common with the region (for a minimum m, px + qy < m).
  • Method: formulate → draw each boundary line → shade the region → list corners (solve pairs of lines) → evaluate Z → test if unbounded → answer in the words of the question.
  • Advantages: optimal use of limited resources; limitations: linearity and divisibility assumptions, a single objective.

FormulaeLinear programming at a glance

TaskRuleNote
Corner of two linessolve a1x + b1y = c1, a2x + b2y = c2never read it off the graph
Which side?substitute (0, 0): true ⇒ origin sideuse (1, 0) if the line passes through O
Two optimal corners (x1, y1), (x2, y2)px1 + qy1 = px2 + qy2gives p : q
Unbounded, max Mpx + qy > M must miss the regionelse no maximum
Unbounded, min mpx + qy < m must miss the regionelse no minimum

Worked examples

Worked exampleConstraints from a graph, optimise, then unbound it (specimen 2027 Q9)

L1 C3

The feasible region is the triangle A(1, 1), B(3, 3), C(1, 7) shown. (a) Write its constraints. (b) Maximise Z = x + y. (c) Change one constraint to make the region unbounded.

Show working
  1. (a) The line through (0, 9) and (9/2, 0) is 2x + y = 9; the others are y = x and x = 1. The region lies below 2x + y = 9, above y = x and right of x = 1: 2x + y ≤ 9, y ≥ x, x ≥ 1.
  2. (b) Z(A) = 2, Z(B) = 6, Z(C) = 8.
  3. (c) Reversing 2x + y ≤ 9 to 2x + y ≥ 9 leaves the region above that line, between y = x and x = 1 — unbounded.

Answer constraints 2x + y ≤ 9, y ≥ x, x ≥ 1; Zmax = 8 at C(1, 7)

Worked exampleA word problem (B2026 Q22)

L2 C3

A dealer has ₹5,760 and room for 20 items. Electronic machines cost ₹360 and give ₹22 profit; manual ones cost ₹240 and give ₹18. How many of each maximise profit?

Show working
  1. x electronic, y manual: x + y ≤ 20, 360x + 240y ≤ 5760 (3x + 2y ≤ 48), x, y ≥ 0; maximise Z = 22x + 18y.
  2. Corners (0, 0), (16, 0), (8, 12) [from x + y = 20 and 3x + 2y = 48], (0, 20).
  3. Z: 0, 352, 176 + 216 = 392, 360.

Answer 8 electronic and 12 manual; profit ₹392

Worked exampleEqual optimum at two corners (specimen 2027 Q1(xiii))

L3 A1

Z = ax + by (a, b > 0) is maximum at both (8, 10) and (7, 12), and ab = 72. Find a, b and Zmax.

Show working
  1. 8a + 10b = 7a + 12b ⇒ a = 2b; 2b2 = 72 ⇒ b = 6.

Answer a = 12, b = 6, Zmax = 156

Worked exampleA minimum over an unbounded region (specimen 2021 Q22(b), diet)

L4 C3

Minimise Z = 20x + 40y subject to 6x + y ≥ 18, x + 4y ≥ 12, 2x + y ≥ 10, x, y ≥ 0.

Show working
  1. Corners: (0, 18); (2, 6) from 6x + y = 18 and 2x + y = 10; (4, 2) from 2x + y = 10 and x + 4y = 12; (12, 0).
  2. Z: 720, 280, 160, 240. Smallest 160 at (4, 2).
  3. The region is unbounded: check 20x + 40y < 160, i.e. x + 2y < 8. That half-plane lies below the dashed line, which touches the region only at (4, 2): no common point.

Answer Zmin = 160 at (4, 2)

Worked exampleLPP theory statements (specimen 2027 Q1(xiv))

L5 A1

S1: every LPP has at least one optimal solution. S2: if an LPP has two optimal solutions it has infinitely many.

Show working
  1. S1 is false: an unbounded region can have no maximum, and an infeasible problem has no solution.
  2. S2 is true: every point of the segment joining two optimal corners gives the same Z.

Answer S1 false, S2 true

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Shading the wrong side of a line: test the origin in each inequality.
  • Reporting a corner value as the maximum on an unbounded region without the half-plane test.
  • Reading a corner off the graph instead of solving the two lines through it.
  • Answering “Z = 392” when the question asks how many of each item.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • C3: constraints read off a drawn region, optimise, then change a constraint so the region becomes unbounded (L1) — the specimen slot; or a word problem with two non-trivial constraints (L2), set in every board 2023–26.
  • A1: the objective equal at two corners (L3) and theory statements (L5).
  • LPP is compulsory in 2027 and worth 5 marks (it was a 4-mark option before).

12 · Probability

Unit 7 · 9 marks · two A1s, a 2-mark counting/independence question and a 5-mark Bayes case study

ConceptConditional probability and independence

  • P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), P(B) > 0. Multiplication theorem: P(A ∩ B) = P(B)P(A|B) = P(A)P(B|A).
  • A, B independent ⇔ P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) ⇔ P(A|B) = P(A). Then A′ and B, A and B′, A′ and B′ are independent too.
  • Mutually exclusive (A ∩ B = φ) is a different idea: two events with positive probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.
  • At least one of independent events: 1 − P(A′)P(B′)P(C′)…

ConceptTotal probability, Bayes, random variables

  • If E1, …, En partition the sample space: P(A) = Σ P(Ei)P(A|Ei) (total probability).
  • Bayes: P(Ei|A) = P(Ei)P(A|Ei) / Σ P(Ej)P(A|Ej) — the probability of a cause given the effect.
  • A random variable X assigns a number to each outcome. A distribution lists values xi with pi ≥ 0, Σpi = 1. Mean E(X) = Σxipi.
  • Not in 2027: the binomial distribution, variance and standard deviation of a random variable.

DerivationTheorem of total probability

To prove. P(A) = Σ P(Ei)P(A|Ei) for a partition E1, …, En.

  1. A = A ∩ S = (A ∩ E1) ∪ … ∪ (A ∩ En), and these pieces are pairwise disjoint because the Ei are.
  2. Addition rule: P(A) = Σ P(A ∩ Ei); multiplication theorem: P(A ∩ Ei) = P(Ei)P(A|Ei).
P(A) = P(E1)P(A|E1) + … + P(En)P(A|En).

DerivationBayes’ theorem

To prove. P(Ei|A) = P(Ei)P(A|Ei)Σj P(Ej)P(A|Ej).

  1. By definition, P(Ei|A) = P(Ei ∩ A)/P(A).
  2. Numerator by the multiplication theorem: P(Ei)P(A|Ei).
  3. Denominator by total probability.
P(Ei|A) = P(Ei)P(A|Ei)P(E1)P(A|E1) + … + P(En)P(A|En)

Caution the denominator is the same for every i: compute it once, then each posterior is its own branch product divided by it.

DerivationIndependence passes to complements

To prove. A, B independent ⇒ A and B′ independent.

  1. A = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ B′), disjoint: P(A ∩ B′) = P(A) − P(A)P(B).
P(A ∩ B′) = P(A)[1 − P(B)] = P(A)P(B′).

FormulaeProbability at a glance

ResultFormulaNote
AdditionP(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
ComplementP(A′ ∩ B) = P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
ConditionalP(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B)P(A′|B) = 1 − P(A|B)
Exactly one of A, BP(A) + P(B) − 2P(A ∩ B)
Truth-tellers contradictp(1 − q) + q(1 − p)
MeanE(X) = Σxipifair game: E(net gain) = 0

Worked examples

Worked exampleBayes with three sources (specimen 2022 Sem 2 Q7)

P1 D5

Machines X, Y, Z make 20%, 35%, 45% of the bolts; 8%, 6%, 5% of their output is defective. A bolt is defective. Find the probability it came from Y.

Show working
  1. P(D) = 0·20(0·08) + 0·35(0·06) + 0·45(0·05) = 0·016 + 0·021 + 0·0225 = 0·0595.
  2. P(Y|D) = 0·021/0·0595.

Answer P(Y|D) = 6/17

Worked exampleA diagnostic filter (specimen 2027 Q19(ii))

P2 D5

1 e-mail in 1500 is harmful. The filter flags 97% of harmful e-mails and wrongly flags 3% of safe ones. (a) P(an e-mail is safe). (b) P(a harmful e-mail is passed). (c) P(an e-mail is safe, given that it is flagged).

Show working
  1. (a) 1 − 1/1500.
  2. (b) 1 − 0·97.
  3. (c) P(flagged) = (1/1500)(0·97) + (1499/1500)(0·03) = (0·97 + 44·97)/1500 = 45·94/1500.
  4. P(S|flagged) = 44·97/45·94.

Answer (a) 1499/1500; (b) 0·03; (c) 4497/4594 ≈ 0·979 — almost every flagged e-mail is safe, because harmful ones are so rare

Worked exampleThe three-door game (specimen 2027 Q19(i))

P3 D5

A laptop is behind one of doors A, B, C. You choose A; the host, who knows, opens B and shows it empty. Should you switch to C?

Show working
  1. P(host opens B | laptop at A) = ½, | at B = 0, | at C = 1.
  2. P(B opened) = ⅓(½) + ⅓(0) + ⅓(1) = ½.
  3. P(A | B opened) = (⅙)/(½); P(C | B opened) = (⅓)/(½).

Answer P(A|B opened) = 1/3, P(C|B opened) = 2/3: switch

Worked exampleBoxes of coins (B2019 Q14(a) = specimen 2021 Q14)

P4 D5

Box A has 2 gold and 1 silver coin, B has 1 gold and 2 silver, C has 3 silver. A box is chosen at random and a coin drawn; it is silver. Find the probability that the box was C, and that it was A.

Show working
  1. P(S) = ⅓(⅓ + ⅔ + 1) = ⅔.
  2. P(C|S) = (⅓ · 1)/(⅔); P(A|S) = (⅓ · ⅓)/(⅔).

Answer P(C|S) = 1/2, P(A|S) = 1/6

Worked exampleConditional algebra (specimen 2027 Q1(xv))

P5 A1

P(A) = m, P(B|A′) = 3m, P(B|A) = 6m. Find P(A|B).

Show working
  1. P(A ∩ B) = 6m2; P(B) = 6m2 + 3m(1 − m) = 3m2 + 3m.
  2. P(A|B) = 6m2/(3m(m + 1)).

Answer P(A|B) = 2mm + 1

Worked exampleSum of two conditionals (B2025I Q1(ix))

P6 A1

P(A) = 3/10, P(B) = 2/5, P(A ∪ B) = 3/5. Find P(A|B) + P(B|A).

Show working
  1. P(A ∩ B) = 0·3 + 0·4 − 0·6 = 0·1.
  2. P(A|B) = 0·1/0·4 = ¼, P(B|A) = 0·1/0·3 = ⅓.

Answer sum 7/12

Worked exampleExactly two / at least two (B2023 Q9(ii))

P7 B2

A, B, C solve a problem with probabilities ½, ⅓, ¼ independently. Find P(exactly two solve) and P(at least two solve).

Show working
  1. Exactly two: ½·⅓·¾ + ½·⅔·¼ + ½·⅓·¼ = (3 + 2 + 1)/24.
  2. All three: 1/24.

Answer exactly two 1/4; at least two 7/24

Worked exampleAt least one hit (B2024 Q1(xii))

P8 A1

Four shots hit with probabilities 0·4, 0·3, 0·2, 0·1 independently. P(at least one hit)?

Show working
  1. 1 − (0·6)(0·7)(0·8)(0·9) = 1 − 0·3024.

Answer probability 0·6976

Worked exampleTest for independence (B2026 Q5)

P9 B2

A die has 1, 2, 3 red and 4, 5, 6 green. A = odd number, B = green. Are A and B independent?

Show working
  1. A ∩ B = {5}: P = ⅙.
  2. P(A)P(B) = ½ · ½ = ¼ ≠ ⅙.

Answer not independent

Worked exampleCounting runs (specimen 2027 Q3)

P10 B2

Over 8 days each day is equally likely to be a day of presence or absence. Find P(present on at least 5 consecutive days).

Show working
  1. Count 8-day strings with a run of ≥ 5 presents, by where the first such run starts.
  2. Starting on day 1: days 1–5 present, days 6–8 free: 23 = 8.
  3. Starting on day 2, 3 or 4: the day before is absent, the five days present, the rest free: 22 each, 3 × 4 = 12.
  4. Total 20 of 28 = 256.

Answer probability 5/64

Worked exampleFind k and the mean (specimen 2018 Q10)

P11 A1

P(X = x) = 0·1 for x = 0, kx for x = 1, 2, k(5 − x) for x = 3, 4. Find k and E(X).

Show working
  1. 0·1 + k + 2k + 2k + k = 1 ⇒ k = 0·15.
  2. E(X) = 1(0·15) + 2(0·3) + 3(0·3) + 4(0·15).

Answer k = 0·15, E(X) = 2·25

Worked exampleMissing entries (specimen 2027 Q1(xx))

P12 A1

X takes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with probabilities m, 3m, a, 5m, b. P(X ≤ 2) = 0·28 and P(X ≥ 4) = 0·52. Find P(X = 3).

Show working
  1. 4m = 0·28 ⇒ m = 0·07; 5m + b = 0·52 ⇒ b = 0·17.
  2. a = 1 − 0·28 − 0·52.

Answer P(X = 3) = 0·2

Worked exampleDistribution when drawing without replacement (B2023 Q14)

P13 D5

10 of 30 fruits are rotten. Two are drawn without replacement; X = number of good fruits. Find the distribution and E(X).

Show working
  1. P(X = 0) = (10·9)/(30·29) = 90/870, P(X = 1) = 2(10·20)/870 = 400/870, P(X = 2) = (20·19)/870 = 380/870.
  2. E(X) = (400 + 760)/870.

Answer P = 3/29, 40/87, 38/87; E(X) = 4/3

Worked exampleExpected gain in a stopping game (Heritage 2024 Q13(b))

P14 D5

A die is thrown up to three times, stopping at the first number greater than 4. A win pays ₹5 and each losing throw costs ₹1. Find the expected gain.

Show working
  1. P(win) = ⅓ per throw.
  2. Gains: +5 (⅓), +4 (⅔·⅓ = 2/9), +3 (4/27), −3 (8/27).
  3. E = 5/3 + 8/9 + 12/27 − 24/27 = (45 + 24 + 12 − 24)/27 = 57/27.

Answer E(gain) = 19/9 ≈ ₹2·11

Worked exampleTransfer between bags (B2019 Q10 = specimen 2021 Q10(a))

P15 B2

Bag A has 4 white and 3 black balls, bag B 3 white and 5 black. Two balls are moved from A to B, then one ball is drawn from B. Find P(it is white).

Show working
  1. Moved WW (6/21): B has 5W 5B; WB (12/21): 4W 6B; BB (3/21): 3W 7B.
  2. P(W) = (6/21)(5/10) + (12/21)(4/10) + (3/21)(3/10) = 87/210.

Answer P(white) = 29/70

Worked exampleTruth-tellers (specimen 2023 Q1(xv))

P16 A1

A speaks the truth 60% of the time and B 90%. In what percentage of cases do they contradict each other?

Show working
  1. 0·6(0·1) + 0·4(0·9) = 0·06 + 0·36.

Answer 42%

Common errorsCommon errors

  • Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A) — in Bayes you want the cause given the effect.
  • Treating mutually exclusive events as independent.
  • Probabilities in a distribution that do not add to 1, or a negative k.
  • In a transfer problem, forgetting that bag B now has two more balls.
  • Including variance or a binomial model: both are out of the 2027 theory syllabus.

Question typesMost probable in 2027

  • D5: Bayes in a context — a diagnostic test or filter (P2) or a game-show / informed-host problem (P3), the two halves of specimen Q19; three sources (P1, P4) in every board 2023–26.
  • B2: counting-based probability (P10) or independent events (P7, P9).
  • A1 (two): conditional-probability algebra (P5, P6) and a distribution with a missing entry (P11, P12).
  • Probability falls from 13 to 9 marks; the mean of a random variable (P13, P14) is the furthest the syllabus goes.
